title: The log: Kafka's one big idea
goal: By the end you can describe a Kafka partition as an append-only log with offsets, read it from any offset with assign and seek in Java or Kotlin, and explain why reading never deletes a record.

warmup.q: Your ledger service and your fraud-check service consume the `payments` topic as two consumer groups. The ledger group has read and committed everything. Fraud check is 3,000 records behind. What happens to the records the ledger group has already read?
options: Kafka deletes them as soon as the ledger group commits its offset
They stay until the topic's retention removes them, whoever has read them
Kafka keeps them until the fraud-check group has read them too, then deletes them
Kafka moves them to a backlog that only the fraud-check group can see
warmup.why: Reading never deletes anything in Kafka. Each group keeps one number per partition: the offset of the next record it will read. Records leave only when retention removes old segment files (lesson 2 of this track), on a time or size limit that ignores readers. The first and third options describe a classic message queue, which is the habit to unlearn here.

sections.h: Why a log: one payment, many services that need to hear about it
sections.body:
Your payment service authorizes a card payment of 40.00 EUR. Four other services need to know about it: the ledger, the fraud check, the notification service and the nightly settlement batch. How does the news reach them?

The simplest version is a direct call. After each authorization, the payment service calls all four over HTTP. It works on the first day and breaks in three ways. If the fraud check is down for two minutes, the payment service has to retry, buffer or drop about two minutes of events. If the notification service takes 120 ms to answer, every payment waits 120 ms longer. And when a fifth team wants the events, you change and redeploy the payment service.

The next version puts a message queue in the middle, the way IBM MQ or RabbitMQ is often used. A queue is a server that holds messages until a consumer takes them. The payment service sends each event once and moves on, and a slow or crashed consumer just leaves messages waiting. That fixes the first two problems. But a classic queue deletes a message once a consumer has acknowledged it, and each message goes to one consumer. To feed four services you need four queues, and the payment service writes every event four times. A fifth service starts with nothing, because last week's payments are gone. And when a bug in the fee calculation means you must process yesterday's payments again, the queue can't give them back.

Kafka keeps the events and lets each reader track its own place. The payment service appends each event to the end of a file that only grows. Every event gets a number, its position in that file: 0, 1, 2 and so on. Each reading service remembers one thing, the number of the next event it wants. Reading changes nothing in the file. So four services, or forty, read the same events at their own pace, and a new service can start at event 0.

That growing file is a **log**: an ordered sequence of records that only grows at the end. Keep this picture for the whole track: one file you only append to, and a bookmark per reader. Every later lesson splits this log up, copies it to other machines or reads it in a cleverer way.

A few names before going on. A **record** is one event in the log; in Kafka it has a key, a value, a timestamp and optional headers. A **broker** is a Kafka server, the process that keeps logs on its disk and answers clients over the network. A **producer** is a client that appends records, and a **consumer** is a client that reads them. A **topic** is the name they use, such as `payments`. Kafka stores each topic as one or more **partitions**, and each partition is one log. This lesson uses topics with a single partition, so here topic, partition and log mean the same thing. Lesson 2 of this track splits a topic into many partitions.

sections.h: The broker numbers every record: offsets
sections.body:
Here is a log after the payment service appended five records. You will build exactly this one in the Try-it below:

```text
offset  key      value
0       acct-17  auth 40.00 EUR
1       acct-42  auth 12.50 EUR
2       acct-17  capture 40.00 EUR
3       acct-99  auth 300.00 EUR
4       acct-42  refund 12.50 EUR
```

The number on the left is the record's **offset**: its position in the log, counting from 0. The broker assigns it when the record arrives. The producer never picks it; it learns the number from the broker's reply:

```java
var record = new ProducerRecord<>("payments", "acct-17", "auth 40.00 EUR");
RecordMetadata md = producer.send(record).get();   // waits for the broker's reply
System.out.println(md.offset());                   // the broker chose this number
```

```kotlin
val record = ProducerRecord("payments", "acct-17", "auth 40.00 EUR")
val md = producer.send(record).get()               // waits for the broker's reply
println(md.offset())                               // the broker chose this number
```

Three rules make offsets useful. First, an offset never changes: record 2 is the capture for account 17 today, next week and in every replay. Second, Kafka never reuses an offset within a partition. Even after old records are deleted (lesson 2 of this track shows how), the next record gets the next number: if offsets 0 to 799 existed and the oldest 300 were deleted, the next record still gets 800. Third, nothing is inserted or edited. You can't put a record between 1 and 2, and you can't change record 3. To correct something, you append a new record. That's why the capture and the refund above are records of their own: the log is the history of what happened, in the order it happened.

Together these rules make an offset a permanent name for one record. When a consumer says "I have processed everything before offset 4", or an incident ticket says "look at offset 3", everyone means the same record.

One more number. The **end offset** is the offset the next record will get: 5 in the log above. Kafka's tools call it the log end offset, or LEO. Everything below it exists; nothing at or above it has been written yet.

You have seen this structure before. Oracle writes every change to its redo log before it touches a table, and PostgreSQL does the same with its write-ahead log. Jay Kreps, one of Kafka's creators, built his 2013 essay "The Log" on that idea: if several systems read the same ordered log and apply it the same way, they all end up in the same state. Kafka turns such a log into a service that many systems share.

try.title: Append five payments and read them back
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the single-node broker: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait`. It is ready in about 5 seconds.

Open a shell in it with `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka bash` and run the commands below. They create a one-partition topic, append five keyed payments and read them back with their offsets.
Predict, then run the consumer command a second time. Which offsets come back?
Keep the broker and the shell open. The next Try-its use them.

code.title: inside the kafka container
code.src:
cd /opt/kafka/bin
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic payments --partitions 1

printf 'acct-17:auth 40.00 EUR\nacct-42:auth 12.50 EUR\nacct-17:capture 40.00 EUR\nacct-99:auth 300.00 EUR\nacct-42:refund 12.50 EUR\n' \
  | ./kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic payments \
      --reader-property parse.key=true --reader-property key.separator=:

./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic payments --from-beginning \
  --max-messages 5 --formatter-property print.offset=true --formatter-property print.key=true

try.expect:
```text
Created topic payments.
The consumer rebalance protocol (KIP-848) is production-ready! Set group.protocol=consumer to try it out. ...
Offset:0	acct-17	auth 40.00 EUR
Offset:1	acct-42	auth 12.50 EUR
Offset:2	acct-17	capture 40.00 EUR
Offset:3	acct-99	auth 300.00 EUR
Offset:4	acct-42	refund 12.50 EUR
Processed a total of 5 messages
```
The second run prints the same five lines: the first read removed nothing. The KIP-848 line is a notice the Kafka 4.4 tools print about the new consumer group protocol (lesson 7 of this track). The older `--property` flag still works in 4.4 but is deprecated; `--reader-property` and `--formatter-property` are the new names.

sections.h: A reader's position is one number
sections.body:
Every reader has to remember where it is, so that after a restart it neither skips records nor processes them twice. What is the least it can store?

A classic queue stores state per message: delivered to whom, acknowledged or not. With a million messages and four consumers, that's four million entries for the broker to keep. A log needs far less. Its records are in a fixed order and never change, so a reader that has handled everything before offset 50 can describe its whole state with one number: 50. That number is the reader's **position**, the offset of the next record it will read. Kafka's design doc says it directly: per partition, a consumer's position is a single integer. Reading means asking the broker for records starting at the position, then moving the position past what came back.

A position kept only in memory is lost when the process restarts. So consumers that work together form a **consumer group**: a named set of consumers that read a topic as one, such as the group `ledger`. The group saves its position in Kafka itself, in an internal topic called `__consumer_offsets`. Saving it is a **commit**, and the saved number is the **committed offset**. The `KafkaConsumer` javadoc is clear that it should be the offset of the next record your application will read, not the last one it finished. Get that wrong by one and every restart skips a record or repeats one. Lesson 6 of this track covers commits in depth.

You don't need a group just to read. A consumer can take a partition directly with `assign` and set its position with `seek`:

```java
TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition("payments", 0);   // topic payments, partition 0
consumer.assign(List.of(tp));     // no group: this consumer just takes partition 0
consumer.seek(tp, 50);            // the next poll starts at offset 50
ConsumerRecords<String, String> batch = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
```

```kotlin
val tp = TopicPartition("payments", 0)                    // topic payments, partition 0
consumer.assign(listOf(tp))       // no group: this consumer just takes partition 0
consumer.seek(tp, 50)             // the next poll starts at offset 50
val batch = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))
```

Because a position is only a number, rewinding is cheap. You fixed a bug in the fee calculation and need to recompute yesterday's settlement batch? Seek back and read again. A new reporting service needs history? It starts at the oldest offset Kafka still has. Neither one changes anything for any other reader.

One thing about `poll`: it returns whatever the broker had ready within the timeout, up to `max.poll.records` (500 by default). That can be fewer records than you wanted, or none at all, especially on the first call while the client is still connecting. Code that needs "the next 10 records" has to loop until it has them or a deadline passes. You write that loop in the lab.

sections.h: Reading does not delete, so every reader gets everything
sections.body:
Since no read removes anything, what does? Only **retention**: a limit per topic on how old or how large the data may get. By default Kafka keeps a topic's data for 7 days (`retention.ms` is 604800000 milliseconds) and then deletes the old part, a whole file at a time. Who has read what plays no part. Lesson 2 of this track shows the files and the rules.

Any number of consumer groups can read the same partition, and each group gets every record. Your ledger service and your fraud check are two groups. Each has its own committed offset, and neither can move the other's.

Several things follow from this, and each one comes back later in this track.

A slow consumer does not slow down the producer or the other groups. It just falls behind. The distance between the end offset and a group's committed offset is its **lag**. If the end offset is 1,250 and the fraud check has committed 40, its lag is 1,210 records.

A consumer that crashes starts again from its last committed offset. Whatever it processed after that commit, it processes again. Kafka's default promise is therefore **at-least-once** delivery: every record is processed at least once, and some may be processed twice. That is why payment consumers need idempotency keys.

Replay is cheap and safe. A new group can read a topic from the oldest offset still kept, and an existing group can move its committed offset back.

Order exists only inside one partition. Two partitions are two separate logs, and nothing orders a record in one against a record in the other. Lesson 2 of this track deals with that.

Kafka 4.2 made share groups production-ready: they hand each record to one member of a group and acknowledge records one by one, like a queue, on top of a topic. Lesson 12 of this track covers them. Every lesson before that uses ordinary consumer groups, which work as described here.

steps: In the container shell, read all five payments as group `ledger` and two of them as group `fraud-check`, then describe both groups (first block below).

sections.h: Why appending is fast: sequential I/O and the page cache
sections.body:
A busy broker might take 50,000 records a second. Can a disk keep up with that?

It depends on where the writes go. A spinning disk has to move its head to the right track before each write, and a seek takes about 5 to 10 ms, so random writes top out at a few hundred per second. Writing at the end of one file needs almost no seeking: the head stays where it is and the data streams on. Kafka's design doc gives the numbers from its test disks: about 600 MB/s for linear writes against about 100 kB/s for random ones. An NVMe SSD narrows the gap a lot (a random 4 KB read takes about 0.1 ms), but sequential I/O still wins, and it lets the operating system do most of the work.

That work happens in the **page cache**: spare RAM in which the kernel keeps copies of recently read and written file data. When the broker appends to a log file, the kernel puts the bytes in the page cache and writes them to disk a little later. When a consumer reads near the end of the log, which describes almost every healthy consumer, the data it wants was written seconds ago and is still in RAM. Copying 4 KB from RAM takes well under a microsecond, against about 100 microseconds from an SSD.

Kafka does not keep its own cache of records on the JVM heap; it leans on the page cache. That's why brokers usually run with a heap of a few gigabytes on machines with far more RAM: the rest is page cache.

Two more choices keep the cost down. Records travel in **batches**: the producer groups records that go to the same partition, and in the common case the broker stores the batch as it arrived and hands it to consumers the same way. And when it can, the broker uses the `sendfile` system call to send file data from the page cache straight to the network socket, without copying it through the JVM. That zero-copy path is not used when TLS is on, because encryption has to happen in user space.

Finding a record is cheap too. An append is O(1): it goes at the end, however long the log is. A read at an offset finds the right file, looks up a small index and reads forward. Lesson 2 of this track opens those files.

The weak spot is a consumer that falls far behind. It reads old data that is no longer in the page cache, so those reads go to disk and can push recent pages out of memory. One lagging batch job can slow down every reader of the tail on the same broker.

analogy: A partition is a bank's ledger book written in pen. Every line has a number, and new lines go at the bottom. Nobody erases a line: a correction is a new line. Each team that reads the book keeps its own bookmark, and moving your bookmark changes nothing for anyone else. Now and then the archive tears out the oldest pages, whole pages at a time, whether or not anyone has read them. The analogy breaks at scale: a topic is many such books written at the same time, each with its own line numbers, and nothing orders a line in one book against a line in another.
in_your_world: Your Quarkus payment services already run on this model. The `payments` topic is the ledger of record, and settlement, fraud check and notifications are separate consumer groups with separate committed offsets, so a slow notification service never holds up settlement. When a fee bug ships and you must recompute a day of settlements, nobody has to re-send anything. You stop the settlement group and move its offsets back with `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets`, or you run a one-off job that assigns the partitions and seeks. A Temporal workflow started by a payment event can store that event's topic, partition and offset, which gives an incident review an exact pointer back into the history.
mistake: Treating a topic as a queue that empties itself. A team publishes full card numbers to a topic because "the tokenizer consumes them and then they're gone". Nothing removes them. They stay in the log for the full `retention.ms` (7 days by default), on every replica, readable by any client allowed to read the topic, and they come back in every replay. People make this mistake because the client API looks like a queue: poll, process, commit. The fix is to choose retention on purpose for every topic and to keep data you may not store for days out of Kafka: tokenize before you produce, or encrypt the field.

compare.title: Read ten records from offset 50 in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java

kotlin.title: Kotlin

compare.note: Both call the same Java client library. Kotlin uses `listOf` where Java uses `List.of`, adds a whole list with `+=`, and uses `take` to stop at ten. `records(tp)` returns a Java `List`, so Kotlin's collection functions work on it directly. Neither version commits anything: with `assign` and no `group.id` there is no group to commit to.

worked.title: Replay one partition from offset 50 up to where it ended when you started

steps.say: A reconciliation job must re-read partition 0 of `payments` from offset 50 and stop at the end. But the end moves: producers keep appending while you read. So pin it first, by asking for the end offset before reading anything.
steps.alt_code:
// 1. pin the end: the offset the next record would get, right now
val tp = TopicPartition("payments", 0)
consumer.assign(listOf(tp))
val stopAt = consumer.endOffsets(listOf(tp)).getValue(tp)

steps.say: Set the position. `seek` only changes a number inside the client; the next `poll` fetches from there.

Read until the position reaches the pinned end. `consumer.position(tp)` is the offset of the next record the consumer will return, which makes it the natural stop condition. Records at `stopAt` or later arrived after you started; leave them for the next run.

Notice what is missing: no `group.id` and no commit. If the job crashes, you run it again from 50. For a one-off replay that is the simplest correct design. A job that must resume where it stopped needs a group and commits, which is lesson 6 of this track.

lab.title: Build a log in memory, then read a real one
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder. All 12 fail: the stubs throw `NotImplementedError` or `UnsupportedOperationException`. The first run also pulls the `apache/kafka-native:4.4.0` image (about 150 MB) for the broker tests; after that the broker starts in a second or two.

In `MiniLog.kt`, write `endOffset`, `append` and `read`. Offsets are dense and start at 0, so the next offset is the number of records so far. `read` returns a copy and rejects a `from` outside `0..endOffset`.
Write `LogReader.poll` and `LogReader.seek`. A reader's whole state is `position`: read from it, then move it forward by the number of records you got.
Run the tests. The eight tests in `MiniLogTest` should pass now.
In `OffsetReader.java`, write `readFrom`: `assign`, `seek`, then a `poll` loop with a deadline that keeps at most `max` records.
Run the tests until all 12 pass. `OffsetReaderTest` runs your code against a real Kafka 4.4 broker in a container.
hints: `records.subList(a, b)` is a view of the list. Wrap it with `.toList()` so a caller never sees later appends through it.

In `readFrom`, `consumer.poll(...).records(tp)` gives you only that partition's records. The loop needs two exits: enough records, or the deadline passed. Without the deadline, a read at the end of the partition never returns.
If only the broker tests fail with a Docker error, check that Docker Desktop is running. `MiniLogTest` needs no Docker.

drill.title: Write the replay loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson. Write `replay(consumer, topic, partition, from)`: it reads one partition from offset `from` up to the end offset as it was when the function started, and returns the values in order. No group, no commits. Then compare with the answer. Did you pin the end offset before the loop?

recap: A partition is a log: an ordered list of records that only grows at the end. The broker gives each record the next offset, starting at 0.
An offset never changes and is never reused within a partition, so it names one record for good.
A reader's state is one number per partition: the offset of the next record. A group saves it in `__consumer_offsets` as its committed offset.
Reading never deletes. Retention removes old data by time or size, whoever has read it.
`assign` plus `seek` reads from any offset without a group, so replay costs nothing.
Appends and tail reads are sequential and mostly served from the page cache, which is why the log is fast.

quiz.q: A partition holds offsets 0 to 799. Retention then deletes the oldest 300 records, and a producer sends one new record. Which offset does it get?
options: 0, because the log is empty enough to start again
quiz.why: Offsets are never reused. The next record always gets the end offset, 800, however much old data retention removed. 500 is the tempting answer if you think of an offset as a position among the records that are left.

quiz.q: Three consumer groups read partition 0 of `payments`, whose end offset is 1,250. Their committed offsets are 1,200 (group A), 900 (group B) and 40 (group C). Which statement is true?
options: Records 0 to 39 can be deleted now, because every group has read them
Group C's lag is 1,210, and its slowness does not hold back groups A and B
Kafka slows the producer down until group C catches up
Group A's commit hides records below 1,200 from the other groups
quiz.why: Lag is the end offset minus the committed offset: 1,250 minus 40 is 1,210. Groups never share positions, and consumers put no back-pressure on producers. Reads delete nothing either: retention decides when records go.

quiz.q: Your code calls `assign` for partition 0, then `seek(tp, 50)`, then a single `poll(Duration.ofMillis(10))`. Offsets 50 to 99 exist, but the poll returns no records. What is the most likely reason?
options: `seek` failed silently and the consumer is back at offset 0
A poll returns only what arrived within its timeout; 10 ms was too short for the first fetch, so poll again in a loop
Offsets 50 to 99 were deleted when another consumer read them
`assign` only works when `group.id` is set
quiz.why: `poll` returns whatever the client has received when the timeout runs out. On the first call the client still has to find the partition leader and send its first fetch, which can take longer than 10 ms. Correct code polls in a loop until it has what it needs or a deadline passes. Reading deletes nothing, and `assign` needs no group.

quiz.q: A team says: "We can't add the new fraud-model service. It would consume the payments and the ledger service would miss them." What do you tell them?
options: Give the new service its own consumer group: each group reads every record and keeps its own offsets
They're right: copy the topic for the new service first
Put both services in one consumer group so they share the records
Only one consumer can ever read a partition, so add partitions first
quiz.why: Reading doesn't consume. A new group gets its own committed offsets and reads every record without touching the ledger group. Putting both services in one group is the real mistake: within a group each partition goes to one member, so each service would see only part of the data. The last option mixes up one member per partition inside a group with one reader per partition overall.

quiz.q: Kafka keeps no cache of records on its JVM heap. Why do most consumers still get their data from memory rather than disk?
options: The JIT compiler keeps hot records in CPU registers
Each consumer keeps a full local copy of the partition
The broker loads every partition into its heap at start-up
The kernel's page cache holds recently written file pages, and most consumers read near the end of the log
quiz.why: Kafka writes segment files and lets the operating system cache them. A consumer near the tail reads pages that were just written and are still in RAM. A consumer far behind reads cold pages from disk, which is why one lagging job can slow down a broker.

flashcards.front: What is an offset in Kafka?
flashcards.back: A record's position in one partition's log: 0 for the first record, then 1, 2, 3. The broker assigns it, and it never changes.

flashcards.front: What is a partition's end offset?
flashcards.back: The offset the next appended record will get. A partition holding offsets 0 to 4 has end offset 5.

flashcards.front: What does a consumer group store for each partition?
flashcards.back: One number, its committed offset: the offset of the next record it will read. It lives in the `__consumer_offsets` topic.

flashcards.front: What happens to a record after every consumer group has read it?
flashcards.back: Nothing. It stays until retention deletes its segment (by default after 7 days).

flashcards.front: How do you read partition 0 from offset 50 without a consumer group?
flashcards.back: `consumer.assign(List.of(tp))`, then `consumer.seek(tp, 50)`, then `poll` in a loop until you have enough or a deadline passes.
For one partition: the end offset minus the group's committed offset. The number of records the group still has to read.

terms.plain: An ordered sequence of records that only grows at the end. Each Kafka partition is one.
A record's number within one partition, assigned by the broker: 0, 1, 2 and so on. Never changed, never reused.
The offset the next record will get. The tools call it the log end offset.
The position a consumer group has saved for a partition: the offset of the next record it will read.
A set of consumers that share the reading of a topic, with one committed offset per partition.
End offset minus committed offset: how many records a group still has to read.
Memory the kernel uses to keep file contents. Kafka relies on it instead of caching records on the heap.

explain_back.prompt: A colleague who has used IBM MQ for years asks: "When my consumer acknowledges a Kafka message, where does the message go?" Explain what really happens, and what decides when the record is deleted.
explain_back.answer: It goes nowhere. Acknowledging in Kafka means committing an offset: the consumer group saves one number per partition, the offset of the next record it will read. The record stays in the partition's log at the same offset, and every other group can still read it, now or later. Kafka deletes old records only through retention, by time (7 days by default) or by size, a whole segment file at a time. So a commit changes only where your group resumes after a restart, and a replay is just moving that number back.

deeper.body:
Jay Kreps' 2013 essay "The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction" is worth an evening. (It was published on the LinkedIn engineering blog. The original page has moved, so search for the title.) Its core argument: a log is the simplest structure that gives you a total order of events, and any deterministic process that reads the same log from the same starting point ends up in the same state. Databases already work this way inside. Replication is mostly shipping the log to another machine.

Two ideas from that line of thinking come back later in this track. A table is a log folded down to the latest value per key: Kafka Streams calls this the stream-table duality (lesson 10), and log compaction (lesson 2) keeps exactly that latest value per key on disk. And change data capture turns a database's own log into Kafka records (lesson 11): Debezium reads the PostgreSQL write-ahead log, or the Oracle redo log through LogMiner, and publishes each change in commit order.

One detail to keep straight: an offset is a logical number, not a byte position. Records vary in size, so the broker can't compute where offset 50 starts in the file. Each segment file has a sparse index from offsets to byte positions, and lesson 2 of this track opens it.
